info.title: ResourcePack AI API
info.description:
Create packs, generate blocks, models, items, GUIs, icons and sounds into them, and download the result.

Every generation is asynchronous: the endpoint answers 202 with a job handle and you poll it. Calls spend the same AI Credits the app does.

get.description:
Page until `nextCursor` is null. An asset's `id` is also its job handle, so this is how you find the handle for something generated in an earlier run.

Every asset says what it is in `type` — `block`, `item`, `item3d`, `gui`, `hud`, `dialog`, `icon`, `sound` and so on — and that is the field to filter and branch on. `kind` is the file format it is stored as (`texture`, `model`, `font`, `sound`), which several types share: a block, an item sprite, a GUI, a HUD and a dialog are all `texture`s. Some types are parts of another asset rather than assets of their own (`block_face`, `model_texture`, `item_model`).

post.description:
Puts a file you already have into the pack — the Studio's Upload button. Free: nothing is generated, though it counts toward the pack's asset limit.

What `file` must be, and what else each `type` needs:

- `block` — a PNG. `target` is the vanilla block texture it replaces (`stone_bricks`); without one it is a texture of your own, named `name`. Square, 1–256px, or send `size` to resample. `faceSlot` with a `target` replaces one face only.
- `item` — a PNG. `target` is the vanilla item it replaces (`diamond_sword`); without one it is a custom item named `name`. Square, 8–256px, or send `size`.
- `icon` — a PNG of any shape, drawn as a chat glyph. Needs `name`. Kept at its own size when 32px tall or less, else 16 tall; `height` overrides it (1–256).
- `model` — Minecraft block model JSON, or a Blockbench `.bbmodel` (its embedded textures come in with it).
- `sound` — Ogg Vorbis, or WAV (converted to Ogg). Needs `event`. MP3 is not accepted; convert it first.
- `gui` — a 256x256 PNG sheet. `target` is the vanilla screen it reskins (`generic_54`, `furnace`…).
- `hud` — a PNG of the HUD sheet, at its own size.
- `armor` — a PNG armour sheet (64x32). `target` is the vanilla set (`iron`, `diamond`…).
- `armor3d` — a Blockbench `.bbmodel` of a 3D armour set.

Images must be PNG. Answers 201 with the asset ready — there is no job to wait for.

get.description:
The asset's own bytes, with the matching content type: PNG for textures and icons, JSON for models, Ogg Vorbis for sounds.

The path takes an asset's `kind` and `name` exactly as the asset listing reports them — `texture/item:rusted_key` for an item sprite, `texture/gui:shop_menu` for a GUI — so copy both from there rather than building them from its type.

Asking before it's ready answers 409 rather than handing back the placeholder that sits there while it generates — a blank PNG that looked like a result is the one genuinely misleading answer available here.

get.description:
A handle looks like `<pack>:<kind>:<name>` and comes back from every generation endpoint. A pack import's is `<pack>:import`, and its answer carries `import` (what came in, what didn't and why) where a generation's carries `asset`.

There's no jobs table behind this: generation is two-phase, so the asset row is written up front with status `generating` and the runner fills it in. The asset *is* the job record, which is why a handle stays resolvable long after the run finished.

Polling always terminates. A run that dies without recording anything reads as `error` once it passes the stale cutoff.

post.description:
Produces a `gui`.

**The easy path is `auto: true`**: a reasoning model plans the whole screen from the prompt — rows, title, materials, buttons, layout — and `target` may be omitted. Without `auto`, you direct everything yourself.

**Image spend**: `elements`, `decorations` and button `icon`s are each their own image call, which is why they share a cap. `texts`, button faces, the title plaque and the frame are composed rather than generated and cost nothing extra.

**Game screens work differently.** `target: "inventory"` is the player's own inventory, which a pack reskins by replacing the vanilla file rather than by overlaying a plugin-opened screen. Vanilla owns its layout, so everything about a menu is ignored there — no title, buttons, cards, elements or decorations — and `auto` only chooses the panel and frame materials. A pack may hold one asset per replaced file; a second is refused with `conflict`.

post.description:
Produces a `hud` — a type of its own beside the GUIs: where a GUI is one screen a plugin opens, this is the overlay drawn over the world while nothing is open at all: hearts, hunger, armor, air, the hotbar, the crosshair, the experience bar and the boss bar.

**There are two sets**, chosen with `hud`. `hud` is what you read while you play; `overlays` is the full-screen layers — the vignette at the edge of your vision, the Nausea swirl. A pack may hold one of each.

**One asset, many files.** A HUD set replaces up to 82 real vanilla sprites and is edited afterwards as a single sheet. A pack may hold ONE of each set; a second is refused with `conflict`.

**Image spend is per GROUP, not per file.** Each group costs one image call, and everything in it is derived from that one drawing — one heart becomes all forty-four of vanilla's moods, fills and damage flashes, and one strip becomes the experience bar and every boss bar colour. Pass `groups` to narrow what you pay for.

**The crosshair is picked, not described.** Vanilla’s stays readable by inverting whatever is behind it, which a resource pack cannot do, so this one is drawn light with a dark outline from a fixed set of shapes. `crosshair` chooses which; a prompt would not survive contact with a snowfield.

post.description:
Produces a `dialog` — the screen a server opens over the game with `/dialog` (Minecraft 1.21.6 and newer), drawn in Minecraft's own look: themed cards, switches, sliders and real clickable buttons.

**The prompt is the whole brief.** A director decides what the screen is — its title, its sections, its controls and its colours (from the pack's style guide when it has one) — and the layout is drawn from that. `layout` narrows which kind of screen it builds; omit it and the director picks.

One flat charge per dialog, refunded in full if it fails. Edit the result afterwards in the Studio's dialog editor.

layout.description:
Which kind of screen to build. Omit for the director's choice.

- `sidebar`: Categories down the left, the chosen one on the right: stores, profiles, menus with sections.
- `columns`: Two to four things side by side to compare: ranks, kits, crates, plans.
- `tiles`: A grid of clickable cards with a state you can read at a glance: rewards, shops, perks.
- `rows`: A list of clickable rows with a value chip: settings, toggles, warps.
- `guide`: A page to read, with its contents down the left: rules, getting started, patch notes.
- `simple`: A few words and one or two buttons: notices, confirmations.

post.summary: Get a URL to upload a file to
post.description:
For a file too big to send inline — a whole pack — or one you have on disk and would rather not base64. Ask with the file's exact length, `PUT` the bytes to `url` with the `Content-Length` it names (`curl -T pack.zip "<url>"` does both), then pass `{"upload": "<upload>"}` as the `file` of the call that wants it.

The URL takes exactly `size` bytes and expires after fifteen minutes. An upload is used once: the call that consumes it deletes it.

post.description:
A resource pack `.zip` — yours, or one from anywhere — as a new pack: the Studio's Import button. It always creates a pack, named after the zip unless you give `name`, at the Minecraft version its `pack.mcmeta` declares unless you give `minecraftVersion`. Free.

Send the zip as an `upload` (see `POST /uploads`) unless it's small. A file that isn't a resource pack at all — a shaderpack, a `.rar`, a zip with nothing a pack can hold — is refused with `not_a_pack` before any pack is created.

**This returns as soon as the pack exists; the import runs after.** Poll `job` (`<pack>:import`) at `GET /jobs/{job}` until it leaves `generating` — a large pack takes a few minutes. The finished job carries `import`: what came in, per kind; what was left out and why (entity art, shaders and anything else a pack here can't hold, as the Studio's review screen lists it); and any asset that failed to land.

Block and item textures, models, font glyphs, GUI sheets and sounds come in. Version overlays are read for the pack's version.

post.summary: Check whether content was generated here
post.description:
For marketplaces: check whether files uploaded to you were generated by ResourcePack AI. No API key.

Send up to 256 hashes per call. Each returns a result in the order you sent it, so you can pair answers to files without matching on the hash yourself.

`generated` is definitive. **`no_record` is not a negative** — it means only that the content is not in our registry, never that a human made it.

[The Origin check guide](/api-reference/origin) has how to compute the hash, which you must follow exactly or every lookup misses silently.

Rate limited to 60 requests a minute per address, since there is no key to count instead.

form.description: Which canonicalisation produced the hash. Absent on `no_record`.

kind.description: What sort of asset it was. Absent on `no_record`.

firstSeen.description: ISO 8601 — when this content first left our systems. Absent on `no_record`.

matched.description: How many of them we generated.

get.description:
The same registry, queried k-anonymously — for a marketplace that would rather not send us the content hashes of what its users upload.

Send the first 5 characters of a hash, get back every fingerprint we hold that starts with them, and match the rest locally.

Hashes are computed exactly as for the lookup endpoint, and the same caveat applies: a hit is definitive, a miss is not a negative. See [the Origin check guide](/api-reference/origin).
